questions.question: Give the four arguments for why manufacturing matters more to South Africa than its GDP share suggests.
questions.expected_answer: Value added — manufacturing multiplies the worth of primary produce and keeps the difference inside the country (the case for beneficiation); job quality and multipliers — formal, year-round work where each factory job supports packaging, freight, canteen and retail jobs around it; linkages — backward to farms, forests and mines and forward to the services that move, sell and finance the goods; and export diversification — manufactured exports, led by the vehicle plants, spread export risk so no single commodity price can sink the economy.

questions.question: Using transport-cost logic, explain why a fish cannery and a soft-drink bottling plant locate at opposite ends of their supply chains.
questions.expected_answer: The plant sits at the end that costs more to move. Fresh fish spoils within hours and shrinks to a fraction of its weight in cans, so canneries locate at the catch — St Helena Bay — and ship the light, durable tins: raw-material orientation. A bottler's input is cheap-to-move concentrate, but its output is crates of heavy, fragile full bottles, so bottling lines locate in the cities that drink them: market orientation. Ask which end is heavier, bulkier or quicker to spoil; the factory parks at the difficult end.

questions.question: List the main factors hindering industrial development in South Africa, including the two structural problems the syllabus names.
questions.expected_answer: Electricity insecurity (load-shedding), decaying rail and congested ports, water cuts, shortages of artisans and engineers worsened by emigration, strikes and adversarial labour relations, crime and corruption (cable theft, extortion, rigged procurement), cheap import competition, and distance from world markets. The two structural problems: over-concentration — industry piled into four core regions, raising congestion, land prices and pollution there while other regions lack investment — and industrial pollution itself, such as the Vaal Triangle's smoke and south Durban's refinery fumes, with carbon-intensive output increasingly taxed at green borders.
